articles.headline: Disney agrees to hire the majority of Character.AI’s workforce
keyFacts: Disney agreed to acquire Character.AI assets for $20 million and offer jobs to at least 60 of its employees following its bankruptcy filing.
A legal filing revealed Character.AI struggled with high costs, potential litigation liabilities, and government child safety investigations.
Because Disney's agreement is a stalking horse bid, another company could still step forward with a higher offer.
body: After chatbot startup Character.AI filed for bankruptcy earlier this week, many of its employees will have the opportunity to take jobs at Disney.
Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand recently became the entertainment giant’s first CTO, and the startup previously said that Disney had agreed to acquire some of its assets for $20 million.

A legal filing spotted by Bloomberg revealed more details about the agreement between Character.AI and Disney, with Disney agreeing to make employment offers to at least 60 Character.AI employees — the majority of the workforce — paying them an estimated $60 million in annual compensation.

The filing also says that the “vast majority” of Character.AI employees who were offered jobs at Disney accepted them. However, this is a stalking horse bid, so another company could come forward with a higher offer.

The filing says that despite its “large and engaged user base,” Character.AI has been hobbled by high costs and “potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement.” (The company was sued by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who said her son became obsessed with one of Character.AI’s chatbots before committing suicide; it also faces government investigations over child safety concerns.)

articles.headline: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
keyFacts: Anthropic granted nonprofit evaluator METR employee-like access to its systems to assess risks of its artificial intelligence models.
The announcement marks the first step in implementing a proposal backed by rivals Sam Altman and Elon Musk.
Critics argued third-party evaluators create conflicts of interest, while Anthropic said public sharing could benefit malicious actors.
body: Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee-like access” to assess the risks of its models, following through on a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control.

METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems.

A greater role for third-party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei achieved a rare moment of unity with arch-rivals Sam Altman and Elon Musk in September when the OpenAI and SpaceX bosses rallied behind his proposal to embed external auditors in the leading labs.
Thursday’s announcement marks the first step to implementing these pledges. OpenAI has yet to lay out plans to bring in evaluators after Altman said Amodei’s proposals were a good idea.

“As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessment,” Anthropic said on Thursday. “We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work.”

Critics of Anthropic’s proposal to use evaluators have argued the arrangements could lead to conflicts of interest, pointing to issues in the accounting sector, and that greater government regulation is required.

Anthropic argued that sharing information publicly could benefit malicious actors or competitors and added that its evaluators will operate similarly to bank supervision, whereby regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks.

articles.headline: The PlayStation 6’s Memory Components Alone Could Cost More Than $700
keyFacts: An insider stated that the memory components for the PlayStation 6 could cost over $700.
The artificial intelligence industry is driving up hardware component costs by requiring monumental resources.
Console manufacturers can no longer rely on traditional game sales to subsidize manufacturing losses.
body: The next generation of home consoles is in constant fluctuation. Studio monopolies are caving in. Players are not on board with the all-digital future. One thing that is certain is that when Sony and Microsoft do pull the trigger, it will be monumentally expensive for players. With costs rising all over, consumer technology is among the fastest climbing expenses, with the AI boom hoovering up key computer components. According to one insider, the PlayStation 6âs memory alone will rake up more than $700 USD, pushing the full price tag over the $1,000 rim.

According to Video Games Chronicle, AMD insider and forum poster âKeplerL2â believes that RAM and flash storage on Sonyâs next console will cost “over $680.” Itâs a startling number, a figure that once upon a time accounted for the entire package, but not a surprising one. Anyone who has had to pluck a quick SSD can attest how rapidly hardware costs have risen in the last three years.

The prime mover in these mounting costs is the AI industry. These firms require monumental resources to dress a baby like a cop for TikTok videos. Before cement is even poured for data centers, companies are calling dibs on key suppliers like NVIDIA, meaning the costs youâre experiencing now is still a phantom to whatâs to come. Itâs forced many tech leaders, especially in the gaming space, to talk out of both sides of their mouth. Epicâs Tim Sweeney and Xboxâs Asha Sharma are laying the groundwork for gamingâs AI revolution five days of the week and admitting itâll lock out swaths of players on the sixth.

Even before Sonyâs post-disc hostilities and fly by night tariffs, the very nature of the console market has shifted considerably. Once upon a time, these companies were willing to bite a loss on manufacturing, knowing they would make up for it with game sales and licensing fees. For over a generation, trends have shifted. Now the average player spends more time with fewer games. Subsidizing that loss with traditional game sales is no longer a guarantee. It has prompted the likes of Sony to focus its attention towards ventures like cross-media development and aspirations to take the live service space for themselves.

Already the current generation of consoles, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and Nintendo Switch 2, are the first to uniformly become more expensive over time instead of less. How much further these costs will hike, and who will be able to keep up, is still in the making.

articles.headline: Quentin Tarantino Says He's 'Written a Script' for 10th and Final Film, But He Wants to 'Live' Before Making It
keyFacts: Filmmaker Quentin Tarantino confirmed during an appearance on The Graham Norton Show that he has written a script for his tenth and final movie.
Tarantino stated he plans to work on his upcoming West End play, spend time with his family, and live a little before making the film.
It remains unannounced when Tarantino will begin production or release the final film, as no official timeline was provided.
body: Quentin Tarantino has confirmed he's "written a script" for his 10th and final film, but he's going to "live" a little before making it.

The Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood and Kill Bill filmmaker teased his plans for his long-in-development finale movie during an appearance on The Graham Norton Show . He said he has a script for a film he "could" do, and it's one he also happens to "really, really like," but he's got a checklist of things to take care of before diving into it.
"I've written a script that I could do that I really, really like, but I have to do the play and see who I am, right?" Tarantino said, referencing his upcoming West End play, The Popinjay Cavalier.
"I'll finish the play, and then I'll go back, be with my family for a while, and then live and then see what that guy wants to do."

The director's words were in response to a question from show host Graham Norton, who asked about his "10th" and "final film." Tarantino didn't skip a beat when conjuring up his reply, suggesting that, yes, the plan is still for his next film to be his last whenever it does eventually hit screens.

For reference, The Popinjay Cavalier is set to start previews February 23, 2027, and then open one month later, March 18. That means we've got some waiting to do before Tarantino will begin the "then live" phase of his pre-movie plan. How long it will be before he then decides on a script, begins production, and settles on a release date remains to be seen, but don't expect to hear any significant updates for a while.

Tarantino mentioned wanting to finish his career as a movie director at film number 10 a few years before the release of his eighth film, The Hateful Eight , in 2014. As Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood came and went as his ninth project in 2019, his decision to put a cap on his big-screen presence has only become more controversial amongst fans.

A filmmaker with a very specific number of trend-setters – including Pulp Fiction , Inglourious Basterds , and Django Unchained – the idea of intentionally ending his time as an artist has been deemed confusing and disappointing. That doesn't seem to have phased Tarantino one bit, and the time it's taken for him to get started on the final project suggests he's not in any rush to get started.

Rumors surrounding his enigmatic 10th once had moviegoers expecting him to direct what Simon Pegg called a "bats**t crazy" Star Trek film before the director eventually debunked those alleged plans himself . He was also once said to be making a project called The Movie Critic before it, too, was scrapped .

It will be some time before Tarantino directs another movie for theaters, but that doesn't mean an opportunity to see his work on the big screen is too far away. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , a Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood follow-up written by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher , will premiere next month .

articles.headline: Scientists Find a ‘Ghostly Green’ Star, and That’s Not the Only Crazy Color
keyFacts: Scientists discovered that white dwarf stars can produce unexpected colors like green, pink, cyan, yellow, and purple, according to a recent study.
Lead author Mark Hollands and his team simulated human vision for 151 white dwarfs, identifying what is likely the first green star ever discovered.
Hollands said most of these stars will shift back to normal colors after a few million years as gravity pulls trace elements inward.
body: High school science class taught us that stars come in very specific colors. You have cooler stars that are red, orange and yellow. Then you have hotter, larger stars that are white and blue. It turns out that much like the wind in the movie Pocahontas, stars also come in all sorts of colors, including green and pink.

The discovery was outlined in a study published this month in RAS Techniques and Instruments. According to the lead author, Mark Hollands of Warwick University’s astronomy and astrophysics group, the humble white dwarf star is the centerpiece of this chromatic curiosity.

“Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs,” Hollands said in a statement. “It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me.”
More from CNET

Hollands says that the key is density and atmosphere. White dwarfs are among the densest objects in the known universe, and that also includes the atmosphere around the white dwarf. Thanks to the intense gravity, a white dwarf’s atmosphere — which is composed primarily of hydrogen and helium — can have some interesting interactions with trace amounts of other elements that are present.

“For white dwarfs with a cool, helium-dominated atmosphere, as the star gets cooler, the helium becomes more and more transparent, which means you can see further into the star where the gas gets denser,” Hollands told CNET in an email. “When you have trace elements in the star, whether it’s metals like sodium and calcium from a planetary system, or carbon from the core, they interact with the dense helium.”

These interactions cause the trace elements to absorb light across the wavelength, for a wider range of “missing” colors. The result is a white dwarf that could appear in any number of colors based on what trace elements it absorbed.
So, there are green stars out there?

That is precisely what Hollands and his team found in their research. To date, no one has ever seen a white dwarf star with human eyes, and none is close enough to be seen directly. Most analysis of a star is done with spectroscopy, so scientists know what a star is made of and how bright it is. Typically, scientists focus more on the science and things like chemical makeup and brightness, rather than color.

“As astronomers, we spend more time thinking about the technical questions about physics,” Hollands said. “It’s a very simple question to ask, ‘what do these stars actually look like when you visit them,’ something I see members of the public ask all the time. It turns out it wasn’t actually too difficult to answer.”

Hollands and his team used the same data for 151 white dwarf stars and ran it through a simulation that converted it to human color vision. Of those, 146 were pretty normal, averaging about 6,800K in color temperature. These would appear bright white to humans, with maybe the tiniest hint of blue.

The other five results were a lot more interesting: The team found examples of cyan, yellow, purple/violet, pink and, yes, even green. The green star is called WD J1330+6435, and it is a white dwarf that sits in a rocky planetary system. The debris from that system gets pulled into the star, lending it the trace elements needed to turn a “ghostly green,” per Hollands.

Another interesting find was WDJ0902+2010, a star that has a ton of carbon in its atmosphere. According to the study, this cooler white dwarf churns up carbon from its innards, and the carbon in the atmosphere absorbs light across the spectrum. It results in a star that would appear salmon-pink to humans.

Since the researchers could find no other credible reports of a green star being discovered before, WD J1330+6435 is likely the first green star ever discovered. Hollands said that the pink and cyan colors were also likely firsts, as there aren’t any reports of astronomers finding stars in those colors either.

Unfortunately, the stars won’t stay in these colors forever. Hollands says that white dwarfs start out intensely hot — about 100,000 degrees Kelvin — which would give them a “sky blue color.” This changes as the white dwarf cools, and you only get the really cool colors when it reaches about 5,000K or so. Eventually, the high gravity will pull the trace elements into the core of the star, changing it back to its normal white or orange colors.

The lone exception is the pink star. Since its carbon already comes from within the star, the star’s natural convection forces are causing that color. That means WDJ0902+2010 is likely to remain pink for billions of years, whereas the rest will likely shift back to their natural colors after a few million years.

articles.headline: Fire Emblem’s Remarkable Comeback
keyFacts: Nintendo's Fire Emblem franchise once faced potential cancellation due to declining sales and franchise fatigue.
The development team stated that Fire Emblem Awakening needed to sell 250,000 copies or the series would end.
Fire Emblem Awakening became a massive hit by adding a Casual mode, saving the series and leading to continued future success.
body: Though it may not be a sales juggernaut on the scale of Mario or The Legend of Zelda, Fire Emblem is one of Nintendo's preeminent franchises. Like so many of its vaunted stablemates, the series is almost as old as Nintendo's gaming ambitions, debuting on the Famicom and appearing on nearly every home and handheld console since. Given this prominence, it's almost difficult to believe that Fire Emblem's future was ever in jeopardy, but such was indeed once the case; there was a point in time when the series was very much on the verge of cancellation, and it took a dramatic shakeup to reverse its fortunes.

To fully contextualize this rocky period in Fire Emblem's history, we need to look back at its trajectory in the wake of its belated international debut. Unlike Nintendo's other marquee properties, Fire Emblem took a circuitous route to Western markets. Though the series began in 1990, its first several installments were never released outside of Japan, and most Western players would end up being introduced to the franchise not through one of its mainline entries, but through Super Smash Bros. Melee for the Nintendo GameCube.

Even more so than its predecessor, Melee was a veritable celebration of Nintendo history. The game drew deeply from the company's rich oeuvre; its roster was stuffed with beloved mascots, and its extensive array of collectible trophies covered the full sweep of the publisher's gaming legacy, from renowned classics to obscure curios. What generated the most chatter among international players, however, were two particular hidden fighters who hailed from a series most had never heard of: Marth, hero of the first Fire Emblem , and Roy, protagonist of the series' then-newest installment, The Binding Blade.

Despite their unfamiliarity, these mysterious swordsmen instantly became two of Melee's most popular characters thanks to their cool designs and nimble swordplay, which helped set them apart from the more recognizable characters on the roster. More consequentially, their newfound popularity among Western players generated immediate interest in Fire Emblem as a whole–a series that, to that point, had been all but unknown outside of Japan. That the franchise was notable enough to warrant not one, but two representatives in Melee was yet more indication of its significance, and only further stoked players' curiosity.
Marth in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate

This upswell in interest (coupled with the critical and commercial success of Fire Emblem's sister series Advance Wars, which likewise had just made its worldwide debut after a similarly long period of Japan exclusivity) went a long way in encouraging Nintendo to finally bring the franchise to other markets, beginning with its next GBA installment (and seventh entry overall), Fire Emblem: The Blazing Blade . The gambit paid off; thanks to its wider availability, Blazing Blade became the first game in the series to sell more than 800,000 copies, solidifying it as another tentpole franchise for the company and ensuring there would be no hesitation to bring future titles westward.

The next few Fire Emblem games saw similar commercial success. The series' second worldwide release (and final GBA installment), The Sacred Stones , arrived in 2005 and moved more than 700,000 copies over its lifetime, while GameCube's Path of Radiance followed later that same year and sold more than half a million copies–well enough to satisfy Nintendo's expectations, considering the system's age and comparatively small user base.

Gradually, however, the series experienced diminishing returns. Fire Emblem: Radiant Dawn , a direct sequel to Path of Radiance, arrived on the Wii in 2007 and ultimately sold fewer copies than its predecessor, despite the fervor surrounding the console at the time. Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon , a DS remake of the original 1990 game, followed in 2008 to a similarly muted reception. While the dual-screen handheld had a significantly larger install base than the Game Boy Advance, Shadow Dragon moved an estimated 600,000 copies–a significant drop off from both GBA titles. In the face of this downward trend, Nintendo elected not to localize the series' next DS entry, New Mystery of the Emblem–the first time in nearly a decade that a Fire Emblem game would not be released outside of Japan.

As with some of Nintendo's other aging franchises from around the same period, franchise fatigue was beginning to set in for Fire Emblem. The relatively quick succession of releases, none of which deviated very far from the series' well-worn formula, coupled with their steep difficulty and lack of innovation, led to a steadily dwindling audience. So persistent was the decline that the long-running franchise now found itself at risk of cancellation; according to the development team, the next Fire Emblem would be the last if it failed to sell at least 250,000 copies, which prompted some radical proposals for how to shake the series up.
Fire Emblem Awakening

The resulting game, Fire Emblem Awakening , did not completely upend fan expectations, but it did become a massive hit, saving the entire series . Rather than reinventing the franchise, Awakening was developed as a "grand culmination" of it, tweaking the established formula in inspired ways and reworking staid conventions. The game leaned heavily on the series' character-driven nature, placing an even greater emphasis on character development and relationships than previous titles. But perhaps even more consequential was the addition of a Casual mode–a feature that originated in New Mystery of the Emblem but had never previously appeared in an international release. Casual mode effectively turned off one of Fire Emblem's hallmark mechanics, permadeath–a move that once felt tantamount to sacrilege, but had a profound impact on the series' approachability. With the option to disable permadeath, the game became much more welcoming; now that there were no long-term repercussions for a miscalculated move, players could enjoy the complex narrative and deep gameplay without worrying about irreversible consequences, opening the series up to a much wider audience than before.

Awakening would go on to sell more than two million copies, kickstarting a resurgence for the series. Each subsequent entry would build upon Awakening's experimental streak, evolving the franchise in unexpected ways. Fire Emblem Fates followed in 2015 and was an even bigger hit, moving more than three million copies. In a page out of Pokemon's playbook, Fates released in three separate versions, presenting the same tale from three alternate perspectives. Two years later, the series made its mobile debut with Fire Emblem Heroes , which would go on to become Nintendo's most successful mobile game, while its final 3DS installment, Fire Emblem Echoes: Shadows of Valentia , followed a few months later and surpassed a million copies over its lifetime.

Fire Emblem has continued to prosper in the years since, with Switch's Three Houses setting a new benchmark for the series with over four million copies sold. Thanks to an eventual willingness to innovate and rethink long-standing conventions, the storied RPG was able to weather declining sales and the looming threat of cancellation to become one of Nintendo's stalwart franchises, offering an incisive lesson in how to steward a long-running series. And with the positive reception that's greeted the newly released Fortune's Weave , it appears Fire Emblem will continue to occupy a vital place in Nintendo's pantheon for a long time to come.

articles.headline: Pope Leo says he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
keyFacts: Pope Leo XIV announced he will gradually resume his duties following surgery to remove a malignant lung tumor.
The surgery was the first major health event of the 71-year-old pontiff's 17-month pontificate and confirmed he had adenocarcinoma.
Doctors are testing the tumor to determine whether the pope will need additional treatments such as chemotherapy.
body: Pope Leo says he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery

VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties.

The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed.

''Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.

The pontiff said the experience of the last week "has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity." He told the faithful that he had ''truly felt your support,'' and expressed ''particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli hospital'' where he was treated.
The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.
A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing.
''He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″

The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

He told a reporter in English that he was doing ''much better'' as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated.

"I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. "It is a miracle that he recovered already."

American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.

''I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,'' Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.''
Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock.

"I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said.

Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place."
"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."

Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.

articles.headline: The dark side of optimizing fertility
keyFacts: Some prospective parents use polygenic screening to test embryos for complex diseases and physical traits, author Kristen V. Brown said.
Most mainstream medical societies and IVF doctors oppose polygenic embryo screening because they believe it lacks value, Brown said.
Embryo editing is currently illegal in the United States and most countries, though interest in the technology is growing, Brown said.
body: A gynecologist points to the head of a fetus in an ultrasound image. | Jan Woitas/picture alliance via Getty Images

We live in an era of endless optimization. Fitness trackers help us measure our lifespan, people are consuming piles of protein in an attempt to be their best selves, and there’s even an urge to maximize our morality . In a world of constant self-improvement, it’s no wonder that journey has reached our attempts at reproduction.

Kristen V. Brown is a journalist and author of the forthcoming book The Immortal Womb: The Centuries-Long Quest to Control the Female Body and Hack Human Reproduction . As the title suggests, she writes about all of the ways people are trying to exert more control over the process of having children.

“I think that what we’re seeing right now is that people will do anything they can to have the healthiest baby possible,” she told Vox. “So much is out of your control, and people are just trying to figure out, how do I get more control? How do I skew the odds in my favor?” She says that one way people try to get more agency is through a technology called PGT-P, or preimplantation genetic testing for polygenic risk.

“If you go through IVF, very often they’ll have you do a basic genetic screening that can detect things like Down syndrome. This screening takes that up a notch,” Brown said. “It uses that same preimplantation genetic testing to look for the likelihood of complex genetic conditions — stuff like heart disease, like diabetes — in order to, quote, ‘let people have the healthiest baby.’”

But what can potential parents do with that knowledge? How far can this technology go? And what are the ethics of using it in the first place? We discuss that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.

Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Brown, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What other things are they testing embryos for?

For conditions that are only impacted by one gene, like Huntington’s disease, it’s very easy to say, ‘Does this embryo have it or not?’ with a pretty good degree of confidence. But that’s not how this technology works. Something like heart disease, for example, is impacted by hundreds of genes. Also, something like heart disease is not only genetic. It’s affected by environment and lifestyle.

I think that what’s motivating most people is the health aspect. But a lot of these companies are marketing these tests, saying they can also look for height. They can look at eye color. Some of them are promising IQ. How do you even define intelligence, let alone how do you define the genetics of intelligence? Alzheimer’s disease, longevity, which embryo is going to live the longest life. So it’s already gone beyond disease into some of these more aesthetic concerns.
Do we know how many people are doing this?
I think it’s a very small number of people at this point. But I think that we’re seeing more and more companies in the space, and we’re seeing more and more support from fertility doctors.

I want to emphasize that most mainstream medical societies are against this. Most of the IVF doctors I know do not think this has value. Most people in the genetic space do not think this technology has value either for embryos or for adults, but I think we’re seeing support growing.
I think that a lot of people in the fertility space are already envisioning a future where this does become more mainstream because the idea is just so appealing, even if the technology has flaws.
What about embryo editing? Is that something we’re seeing? Can people go in and change things around?

Not right now. Embryo editing is very much illegal in the United States. It is illegal in most countries. How can you be sure enough that it’s safe? Because you won’t know for sure until an embryo grows up into an adult whether anything went awry.

Right now it is illegal, but there is growing interest as the technology has gotten better. Most of the support right now for embryo editing is for disease. The argument for it is that, let’s say you are a carrier for Huntington’s disease or you have Huntington’s disease. Right now, there is something that you can do. You can use polygenic screening to select the embryos that don’t have the disease, but in IVF, even if you don’t have a terrible disease hiding in your DNA, it’s hard to get a lot of embryos.

You have these situations where couples have to do rounds and rounds and rounds of IVF to get one or two embryos that aren’t carriers for a harmful variant, right? And so the argument for it is, let’s give these people a better shot.
But I imagine there are people out there who aren’t looking into editing simply for making children more resistant to diseases. They are looking at those things like eye color and height.

There’s actually a name for that. This tech executive called Brian Armstrong coined this term, the Gattaca stack, [named] after the movie. The vision is to use a suite of fertility technologies to make the perfect human.

The first thing they want to use is this technology called in vitro gametogenesis, which is where you take a skin cell and you turn it into an egg and a sperm, and then you make an embryo with it, so women don’t have to go through rounds of IVF.
The idea is that you can get tons and tons and tons of embryos, and then you can use PGT-P to then screen for the best ones, and then you can use an artificial womb to incubate and grow them.
This brings to mind a certain E word, and that word is eugenics. What are the ethics here?

Because on one hand, I can understand that there are parents who are like, “I just want to have a healthy baby. I want to bring a child into this world. I just want to put my best foot forward with this human that I’m going to bring to Earth.” And then on the other hand, it gets a little weird.

It gets weird fast. In some ways, we’ve already gone down that slippery slope. Right now, even if you don’t go through IVF, we screen against Down syndrome early in pregnancy. Down syndrome is a condition in which you have a disability, but you can live a full, happy, healthy life. For a long time, parents of kids with Down syndrome have argued that already selecting and screening against Down syndrome pregnancies is a form of [eugenics].

As technology gets more advanced, we see that same question applied to more and more conditions. I think that one of the things that we don’t talk about enough is that the genome is complicated. You can’t actually just go in there and be like, ‘I want a tall baby with blue eyes and a great laugh.’

I think that becoming a parent is an exercise in giving up control, and that’s easier for some people than others. I have so much sympathy and empathy for people who are trying to stack the deck. But I think there are just so many variables when it comes to human reproduction that we are never going to be able to fully control the process, as much as we might want to and as appealing as that might sound.

articles.headline: Incoming Democrats Avoid ‘Impeach The Motherf**ker’ Rhetoric
keyFacts: Incoming progressive House Democrats are showing little enthusiasm for impeaching President Donald Trump if their party retakes the chamber.
Several vocal Democratic champions of impeachment lost their primary elections, while others question if another impeachment would achieve meaningful accountability.
The House is scheduled to vote next month on an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth forced by Republican Representative Thomas Massie.
body: Hours after Democrats retook the House of Representatives halfway through President Donald Trump’s first term in 2019, Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) made a controversial but true statement.

“We’re gonna go in there and we’re gonna impeach the motherfucker,” Tlaib, a member of an informal group of freshly elected young progressives known as “The Squad,” said at an event hosted by the liberal group MoveOn.
Tlaib faced intense backlash for the remark, with Republicans eager to point at examples of liberal derangement and senior members of the Democratic Party angry at her overeagerness.

Now, with Democrats on the verge of retaking control of the House, a new group of incoming progressive freshmen, already nicknamed “The Bloc,” are decidedly cooler on impeaching the president. It’s a vivid display of how the party and its voters have lost interest in the idea after two failed impeachments even as Trump’s corruption reaches new heights in his second term.
Asked whether she would support impeaching the president, Darializa Avila Chevalier, a socialist and the likely next Democratic member of Congress from New York’s 13th district, said not necessarily.

“That is something that Trump himself seems to want, and so my question is: Is that actually going to be meaningful accountability for the Trump administration?” Chevalier told Politico’s Dasha Burns in an interview posted Friday. “We are going to have to think about what is actually going to hold their feet to the fire.”
Melat Kiros, a socialist who won the Democratic primary for a House seat representing Denver, seconded the sentiment in the same interview.

“I’d have to learn more about what the case would be,” Kiros said. “I think [Trump] has committed multiple impeachable offenses, without question. But I want to make sure, you know, like Darializa said, the accountability has to actually lead to some material changes.”

Meanwhile, the sitting Democrats who’ve most loudly championed impeaching Trump in his second term, Reps. Shri Thanedar of Michigan and Al Green of Texas, both lost their primaries and won’t return to Congress. The incumbent Democrat whom Kiros ousted, Rep. Diana DeGette, touted her work as a House impeachment manager during the campaign to little effect.

And in competitive general election races, impeachment has not been a major topic of discussion, even as President Trump repeatedly complains he’ll get impeached if Democrats win control of the House.

“I can’t speak for everybody else, but I would not support an impeachment of Trump. There’s just simply no reason for that, no matter what happens in the midterms,” former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who is challenging Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) in a bid to return to the Senate, told the Columbus Dispatch this week.

Democrats impeached Trump twice in his first term, in 2019 and then again in 2021, and each time a majority of Senate Republicans voted to acquit him of high crimes and misdemeanors. And he still came back.
Since the first two impeachments had such a seemingly small impact, Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) suggested this week that impeachment is just kind of boring now.
“We’ve seen that movie before. We may have to see it the third time, whether we like it or not. But I don’t think that’s going to get anybody excited,” Schatz told The Bulwark.

MoveOn spokesman Joel Payne said there might be more energy to impeach cabinet officials like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth than to impeach Trump. Still, Payne said MoveOn’s members don’t want impeachment taken off the table.

“There’s a lot of ways to hold folks accountable. I think impeachment is one of them, and I think just from the perspective of our members at MoveOn, our members don’t want to take any of those options off the table,” Payne told HuffPost.

The House is already set to vote on an impeachment resolution against Hegseth next month, as soon as lawmakers return to the campaign trail. But it’s not a Democrat forcing the vote — it’s longtime Trump antagonist Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) — and with at least one Republican in support, the vote will be close, and if it succeeds and Hegseth is impeached, it could scramble impeachment politics next year.
Already, several Democrats have said impeaching Hegseth and other cabinet officials would be a better way to pursue accountability against the administration.

Still, it would be somewhat surprising if there’s really less appetite for impeaching Trump next year considering how much more obviously the president has ignored traditional, legal and constitutional limits on his power, such as by directing prosecutions of political enemies, literally bulldozing the White House, and enriching himself with business ventures that pose a massive conflict of interest.

Kiros suggested voters might care more about presidential accountability if Democrats link political corruption to the broader economy, an idea that’s been common in Democratic messaging this election cycle.

“I think the voters are much more concerned about learning the kind of corruption that has a direct impact on their wallets, that has a direct impact on the way that the economy is growing in a way that is completely concentrated with the billionaires and the corporations, and totally leaving working families behind,” Kiros said.

Democratic leaders in the House have sought to balance the ideal of holding Trump accountable with the reality of what they can actually deliver. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who would likely lead any impeachment inquiries as chair of the House Judiciary Committee next year if Democrats control the House, told HuffPost last month the president has committed a dozen impeachable offenses.
“Democrats in Congress have proven that we are not afraid of impeachment in any way,” Raskin said. “At the same time, having been through the prior two, we also understand it’s not a panacea.”

articles.headline: Oh no, what happened to my OOHPod? Windows command prompt puts in a surprise appearance
keyFacts: An OOHPod postal locker screen in Ireland displayed a Windows command prompt instead of the normal interface during parcel retrieval.
A reader told The Register that tapping the screen opened the prompt, but no keyboard or port was available.
Another tap on the touchscreen restored the normal interface, allowing packages to be collected as usual.
body: The Windows command line is a marvelous thing, beloved by administrators, but not quite so welcome when you're trying to get a parcel out of a locker. Today's example of Windows behaving badly comes from Ireland and one of the nation's OOHPod postal lockers. An eagle-eyed Register reader, trying to retrieve a parcel, found the locker screen instead teasing a command prompt. For the uninitiated, OOHPod is a service where people retrieve and deposit goods in lockers. Scan your ID (or enter it on a touch screen) and the appropriate locker door springs open and the item (or items) can be retrieved. This all works, assuming whatever is running behind the scenes isn't having a bit of a moment, as our reader experienced. Instead of a welcoming display on the locker's screen, our reader found a blank screen and what looked suspiciously like a minimized command-line window. "I tapped to maximize the window," they told us, "and a sudden command prompt appeared immediately afterward." A command prompt? More like an open invitation for mischief for the average Register reader. After all, while ordinary customers might have been flustered, this was surely an opportunity to teach the engineers who allowed it a lesson. Perhaps a cheeky FORMAT, or possibly the creation of a truly cursed batch file? Or something worse? This is surely what the comment section is made for. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on your perspective), no pop-up keyboard appeared for our reader to unleash havoc (not that they would dream of such a thing), and there was no handy socket to plug in a peripheral. The touchscreen accepted another finger jab, and the command window went away, replaced by the usual OOHPod interface, allowing packages to be collected as normal. It was the responsible thing to do, and the bank of lockers was left in a state where the next customer would not have to worry about what this odd cmd.exe thing was all about. However, the question remains. Would you have been so responsible? Or, if there was some way to enter commands, would you have tried to turn a minor bork into a life lesson for the engineer who let Windows give passersby a glimpse of its undercrackers? ®

articles.headline: No further action against government adviser's wife over Palestine Action post, police say
keyFacts: Metropolitan Police officers determined that a social media post by Sarah Helm referencing Palestine Action did not meet the criminal threshold.
Police stated that no further action will be taken regarding the post made by the wife of the government's national security adviser.
Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025, making support for the group a criminal offence.
body: - Published
Police say no further action will be taken against the wife of the government's national security adviser after she posted on social media referencing Palestine Action.
Sarah Helm, who is married to Jonathan Powell, wrote on X on Thursday: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."

She was responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support the proscribed organisation.
On Saturday, the Metropolitan Police said Helm's post was "assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold".
"No further police action will be taken," the force added.

On Friday, the Met Police had said it was "in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required" after it was "made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action".
Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025. Support of the group is a criminal offence and punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Best-selling author Rooney said she would donate earnings from her books to the group, which has a stated goal of "ending global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".
As a result, Rooney's publisher, Faber, determined it could not sell her novels, including Normal People and Conversations with Friends, in the UK.
